metadata.title: THE ROLE OF SUBNATIONAL GOVERNMENTS IN ADULT SKILLS SYSTEMS: SPAIN

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note is a governance and responsibilities mapping for Spain’s adult skills system, not an analysis of student microdata from an ILSA (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIAAC) with sampling weights. The document describes institutional roles across national, regional, and local levels (e.g., ministries, public employment services, chambers of commerce, adult education centres) and summarizes expenditure structure using OECD compilation sources. Because there is no student-level assessment dataset and no estimation of achievement distributions or PV-based outcomes, complex survey weights and replicate weights are not applicable. Any weighting concepts here refer to governance/expenditure shares reported in the note, not to statistical survey inference from an assessment micro-sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the note does not analyze cognitive assessment outcomes from an ILSA/PIAAC-style testing program at the student level. The document is descriptive and institutional (governance structures, responsibilities, and expenditure shares), so there is no PV generation/combination step and no PV-based missingness mechanism to report. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported because no statistical model is estimated on microdata with missing responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used a country-level governance/expenditure compilation for Spain as part of an OECD review of 38 OECD countries; no student-level analytic sample is constructed or filtered.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Spain country note describes how the adult skills system is governed across national, regional, intermediate (provinces), and local levels, and how responsibilities are allocated across major policy areas (VET/HVET, CET, AE, and ALMP). It characterises Spain as a decentralised (quasi-federal) system where the national level sets strategic priorities and frameworks, while regional governments adapt and implement policies, and municipalities play a more limited complementary role. The note also reports the share of general government expenditure at the sub-national level (47.3%) and provides a structured mapping of which level is responsible for strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery. Because the document is not an empirical student-assessment analysis, it does not involve assessment scaling, plausible values, or ML model performance metrics. The implications are therefore institutional: clarifying multi-level governance can inform coordination mechanisms, accountability, and resource alignment across providers and employment services.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML and assessment methodology because the document is a descriptive OECD country note on governance structures rather than an empirical large-scale assessment analysis. There is no student-level dataset, no achievement outcome, and no predictive modeling pipeline to populate fields such as sample size, PV handling, missing-data handling, or ML techniques. As a result, main findings are represented narratively in the outcome summary rather than as ML performance results.
